method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom (whole-page renders plus glyph-level checks of every number and ambiguous token), with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry and caption. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch15 p783-785: auto-generated source checklist from existing 54 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 3x zoom; any printed unit errors or ambiguous glyphs are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. No new medical facts introduced beyond the scan.

elements.source: Alport syndrome is also known as hereditary nephritis and is caused by a mutation in: [Alport syndrome = hereditary nephritis; the mutation is in collagen IV (COL4A5), with deletion as the commonest type. (Book p783)]
Fill up: In Alport syndrome the commonest type of COL4A5 mutation is a ______. [Mutation in collagen IV (COL4A5): the commonest is a deletion. (Book p783)]

Match each type IV collagen heterotrimer with the basement membrane in which it is seen — 1) α1–α1–α2  2) α3–α4–α5  3) α5–α5–α6 … A) Seen from birth  B) Skin basement membrane  C) GBM, cochlea and ocular BM [Type IV collagen table: α1-α1-α2 is seen from birth; α3-α4-α5 is found in the GBM, cochlea and ocular BM; α5-α5-α6 is found in skin basement membrane.]

Alport syndrome damages the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea and ocular basement membrane but the skin basement membrane is spared in the classical form. Which collagen chain combination explains this distribution? [The α3-α4-α5 heterotrimer is seen in the GBM, cochlea and ocular BM — the three sites involved in Alport syndrome. α5-α5-α6 marks skin basement membra]
The α1–α1–α2 collagen IV trimer is present in basement membranes from birth. [The type IV collagen table lists α1-α1-α2 against 'birth'. (Book p783)]
Which site is NOT listed as a location of the α3–α4–α5 collagen IV network? [α3-α4-α5 is seen in GBM, cochlea and ocular BM; skin basement membrane contains α5-α5-α6. (Book p783)]

Match the mode of inheritance with the affected chain in Alport syndrome — 1) X-linked (80%)  2) Autosomal recessive (15%)  3) Autosomal dominant (5%) … A) α3/α4  B) α3/α4  C) α5 [Inheritance table: X-linked (80%) affects the α5 chain; AR (15%) and AD (5%) both affect α3/α4. (Book p783)]

The commonest mode of inheritance in Alport syndrome, X-linked, accounts for: [X-linked inheritance accounts for 80% of Alport syndrome, affecting the α5 chain, with ESRD by 30 years in males and females as carriers. (Book p783)]

A man with X-linked Alport syndrome reaches end-stage renal disease. According to the table, ESRD occurs: [X-linked (80%) Alport syndrome: ESRD by 30 years in males (♂), with females (♀) as carriers. (Book p783)]
In the AR form of Alport syndrome, ESRD occurs by 40 years and affects both females and males. [AR (15%) affects α3/α4 and causes ESRD by 40 years in both ♀ and ♂. (Book p783)]

Match each Alport inheritance pattern with its features — 1) X-linked (80%)  2) Autosomal recessive (15%)  3) Autosomal dominant (5%) … A) ESRD by 30 years in males; females are carriers  B) Mild disease in females and males  C) ESRD by 40 years in females and males [Inheritance table: X-linked (80%, α5) gives ESRD by 30 years in males with females as carriers; AR (15%, α3/α4) gives ESRD by 40 years in both sexes; ]
Fill up: Autosomal dominant Alport syndrome (5%) produces ______ disease in females and males. [AD (5%) Alport syndrome affects α3/α4 and produces mild disease in both females and males. (Book p783)]
Autosomal recessive Alport syndrome accounts for what proportion of cases? [Alport inheritance: X-linked 80%, AR 15%, AD 5%. (Book p783)]

Match the timeline in Alport syndrome with the feature — 1) 5 years  2) 10 years  3) 10–15 years  4) 25–30 years … A) Asymptomatic microhematuria  B) Proteinuria + hypertension  C) ESRD  D) Creatinine rises [Timeline: 5 years asymptomatic microhaematuria; 10 years proteinuria + hypertension; 10–15 years rising creatinine; 25–30 years ESRD. (Book p783)]

A 12-year-old boy with a strong family history of renal failure has a rising serum creatinine. On the clinical-features table, at which point in the timeline does this occur? [The Alport timeline places 'creatinine ↑' at 10–15 years, after microhaematuria at 5 years and proteinuria with HTN at 10 years. (Book p783)]

The earliest renal manifestation in Alport syndrome (5 years) is asymptomatic microhematuria. [Timeline, 5 years: asymptomatic microhaematuria; proteinuria with hypertension appears only at 10 years. (Book p783)]

The ENT manifestation of Alport syndrome at 15 years is sensorineural hearing loss that characteristically begins at: [ENT manifestation at 15 years: SNHL of low frequency (m/c) which subsequently becomes high frequency. (Book p783)]

Fill up: The hearing loss of Alport syndrome is sensorineural, abbreviated ______. [Alport syndrome produces SNHL (sensorineural hearing loss), initially low frequency, later high frequency. (Book p783)]

A 20-year-old man with Alport syndrome is examined at the slit lamp. The pathognomonic ocular sign is: [Ocular manifestations at 20 years: anterior lenticonus (pathognomonic), with an oil droplet appearance on slit lamp. (Book p783)]

Fill up: The pathognomonic ocular manifestation of Alport syndrome is anterior ______. [Anterior lenticonus — marked pathognomonic in the table — with an oil droplet appearance on slit lamp at 20 years. (Book p783)]

The ocular findings described in Alport syndrome are an oil droplet appearance on slit lamp and anterior lenticonus. [Ocular manifestations at 20 years: anterior lenticonus (pathognomonic) and oil droplet appearance on slit lamp. (Book p783)]

All but one of the following appear in the Alport clinical-features timeline. Which is the odd one out? [The 5-year entry is asymptomatic microhaematuria; proteinuria (with HTN) appears at 10 years, and ESRD at 25–30 years. (Book p783)]

A patient with Alport syndrome presents at 27 years with uraemic symptoms — fitting the last row of the clinical-features table, which reads: [The final timeline row of the Alport table is ESRD at 25–30 years. (Book p783)]

elements.source: Match each Alport syndrome finding with the investigation that shows it — 1) Splitting and lamellation of the lamina densa  2) No immune deposits  3) Normal glomerular architecture on routine staining … A) Immunofluorescence  B) Light microscopy  C) Electron microscopy [In Alport syndrome light microscopy and immunofluorescence are normal, the diagnosis resting on electron microscopy, which shows splitting and lamella]

The electron-microscopy appearance described in Alport syndrome is: [EM in Alport syndrome: splitting + lamellation of the lamina densa, alternating thick and thin foci, giving a basket-weave appearance. (Book p784)]

Light microscopy and immunofluorescence are typically normal in Alport syndrome, the diagnosis resting on electron microscopy. [Investigation in Alport syndrome: LM and IF are normal; EM shows splitting/lamellation of the lamina densa with a basket-weave pattern. (Book p784)]
The treatment given for Alport syndrome in the book is: [Rx in Alport syndrome: transplant — with the post-transplant complication of Goodpasture syndrome (antibody against α3). (Book p784)]

What percentage of Alport patients develop Goodpasture syndrome as a complication after transplantation? [Complication post-transplant in Alport syndrome: 5% develop Goodpasture syndrome, from antibodies against α3 (collagen). (Book p784)]

A man with Alport syndrome received a kidney transplant; 8 months later anti-GBM antibody is detected. Which explanation fits the book? [Alport syndrome post-transplant: 5% develop Goodpasture syndrome due to antibody against α3, because the native α3 had never been 'seen' by the immune]
Thin GBM disease is inherited as and caused by: [Thin GBM disease: AD, COL4A4/A3 mutation. (Book p784)]

Match thin GBM disease features with their descriptions — 1) Clinical features  2) Light microscopy and IF  3) Electron microscopy … A) Uniformly thin (<200–300 nm)  B) Normal  C) Microscopic haematuria (<5 years) with good prognosis [Thin GBM disease: microscopic haematuria (<5 years) with good prognosis; LM and IF normal; EM shows a uniformly thin GBM (<200–300 nm). (Book p784)]
On electron microscopy, the glomerular basement membrane in thin GBM disease measures: [EM in thin GBM disease: uniformly thin GBM, <200–300 nm. (Book p784)]

Thin GBM disease usually has a good prognosis, presenting with microscopic haematuria below 5 years of age. [Thin GBM disease clinical features: microscopic haematuria (<5 years) and good prognosis; LM/IF are normal with EM showing a uniformly thin GBM. (Book]

All but one of the following are seen in thin GBM disease. Which is the odd one out? [Basket-weave splitting/lamellation of the lamina densa belongs to Alport syndrome; thin GBM disease simply shows a uniformly thin GBM on EM. (Book p78]
Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disease caused by a defect in: [Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disease caused by a defect in α-galactosidase. (Book p784)]

Match each Fabry feature with its description — 1) Angiokeratoma  2) Accumulation in vessels  3) Renal involvement … A) Appears in the 2nd decade  B) Asymptomatic microhaematuria + proteinuria, the earliest, with ESRD by the 4th–5th decade  C) Heart, cerebrovascular and cornea verticillata [Fabry features: acroparesthesia; angiokeratoma (2nd decade); accumulation in vessels of heart, cerebrovascular system and cornea verticillata; renal —]

The earliest renal abnormality in Fabry disease is: [Renal involvement in Fabry disease: asymptomatic microhaematuria + proteinuria is the earliest, culminating in ESRD by the 4th–5th decade. (Book p784)]
In Fabry disease, ESRD develops by the: [Renal feature of Fabry disease: asymptomatic microhaematuria + proteinuria (earliest) with ESRD by the 4th–5th decade. (Book p784)]

Fill up: The skin lesion of Fabry disease shown in the figure is ______, appearing in the 2nd decade. [Fabry disease produces angiokeratoma (in the 2nd decade), shown in the accompanying figure. (Book p784)]

All but one of the following are listed as sites of vessel accumulation in Fabry disease. Which is the odd one out? [Accumulation in vessels is described for heart, cerebrovascular system and cornea verticillata; the renal features are microhaematuria/proteinuria and]

A 32-year-old man has acroparesthesia, angiokeratomas over the bathing-trunk area and proteinuria. Urine microscopy under polarised light shows lipid deposits. Which investigation matches Fabry disease? [Investigations in Fabry disease: urine shows maltese cross deposits under polarised light; renal biopsy shows vacuolation of podocytes. (Book p784)]

Match each Fabry disease finding with its investigation — 1) Maltese cross deposits  2) Vacuolation of podocytes  3) Angiokeratoma in the 2nd decade … A) Skin examination  B) Renal biopsy  C) Urine under polarised light [Fabry investigations: maltese cross lipid deposits in urine under polarised light and vacuolation of podocytes on renal biopsy; angiokeratoma appears ]

Fill up: The lipid deposits in the urine of Fabry disease appear as ______ crosses under polarised light. [Urine in Fabry disease: maltese cross deposits under polarised light, from lipid-laden cells. (Book p784)]

A young man with Fabry disease has both renal and extrarenal disease. Which extrarenal symptom is listed first among his features? [The features list of Fabry disease begins with acroparesthesia, then angiokeratoma (2nd decade), vessel accumulation in heart/cerebrovascular/cornea, ]
Fabry disease is inherited in an X-linked manner and is a lysosomal storage disorder. [Fabry disease: X-linked lysosomal storage disease due to α-galactosidase defect. (Book p784)]

elements.source: Nail-patella syndrome is inherited as and caused by: [Nail-patella syndrome: AD, LMX1B mutation. (Book p785)]

Match the nail-patella syndrome features — 1) Nails  2) Knee  3) Pelvis X-ray  4) Renal … A) Absent patella  B) Adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria, usually benign  C) Dystrophic nails  D) Iliac horn [Clinical features of nail-patella syndrome: dystrophic nails, absent patella, iliac horn, and renal manifestation — adolescent microhaematuria + prote]

A 16-year-old has microhaematuria and mild proteinuria with absent patellae and dystrophic nails. A pelvic radiograph shows an iliac horn. The renal prognosis is: [Renal manifestation of nail-patella syndrome: adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria, benign, rarely progressing to ESRD. (Book p785)]
Fill up: On X-ray, nail-patella syndrome shows an iliac ______. [Nail-patella syndrome features include the iliac horn, shown in the pelvic radiograph labelled 'iliac horns'. (Book p785)]
The investigation finding on electron microscopy in nail-patella syndrome is: [Investigation in nail-patella syndrome: EM shows a moth-eaten appearance (figure 'moth eaten appearance'). (Book p785)]

Match each familial glomerular syndrome with its electron-microscopy signature — 1) Alport syndrome  2) Thin GBM disease  3) Nail-patella syndrome … A) Uniformly thin basement membrane (<200–300 nm)  B) Moth-eaten appearance  C) Splitting + lamellation of lamina densa (basket weave) [EM signatures: Alport → splitting/lamellation of the lamina densa with basket-weave and alternate thick/thin foci; thin GBM disease → uniformly thin (]

Dystrophic nails and an absent patella are clinical features of nail-patella syndrome along with an iliac horn. [Nail-patella syndrome features: dystrophic nails, absent patella, iliac horn and renal (adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria, benign). (Book p785)]

Nail-patella syndrome's renal involvement (adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria) is classified as: [Renal manifestation of nail-patella syndrome: adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria — benign (rarely progress to ESRD). (Book p785)]

All but one of the following belong to nail-patella syndrome. Which is the odd one out? [Anterior lenticonus is the pathognomonic ocular sign of Alport syndrome; nail-patella syndrome shows dystrophic nails, absent patella, iliac horn and ]
